title: Soup in Six Steps

lines.text: Welcome back to Kitchen Basics. Today we're making a vegetable soup that anyone can cook.
First, wash two carrots, one potato and a large onion. Then cut everything into small pieces.
Put a little oil in a big pot and fry the onion for about five minutes. It should be soft but not brown.
Next, add the carrots and the potato, and stir for another two minutes.
Now pour in a litre of water. Don't use too much, or the soup will taste weak.
Add some salt and a few leaves of fresh basil. If you don't have basil, parsley works well too.
Cover the pot and let it cook for twenty-five minutes. Don't forget to check it now and then.
While it's cooking, you could toast some bread. A bit of cheese on top makes it even better.
When the vegetables are soft, take the pot off the heat and let it cool for a few minutes.
Finally, mix the soup with a blender if you like it smooth. I prefer it with small pieces.
Serve it hot, and enjoy! Next week, we'll make a simple fruit cake.

title: Staying Calm Before Exams

lines.text: You're listening to Mind Matters. This week, we're talking about exam stress. With me is psychologist Doctor Kim.
Thanks for inviting me, Ben. Many students feel anxious before exams, and that's completely normal.
What's the best way to deal with it?
Start early. Students who study a little every day usually feel calmer than those who study all night before the exam.
I'm guilty of that. What else?
Sleep is essential. If you don't get enough sleep, you'll find it harder to remember things.
What about food? I always drink lots of coffee.
I'd avoid that. Too much coffee can make you feel nervous. Try drinking water and eating regular meals instead.
And what should you do in the exam itself?
Read the questions carefully, and begin with the easy ones. If you get stuck, move on and come back later.
Great tips. Any final advice?
Yes. Remember that one exam doesn't decide your future. Be kind to yourself.

title: Strike Day Notice

lines.text: Good morning. This is an important message for all passengers of Westline Railways.
Because of a strike by some of our drivers, there will be fewer trains tomorrow and on Friday.
Only one train an hour will run between Bristol and London, instead of the usual three.
Tickets for tomorrow will be accepted on any day next week, and refunds can be requested online.
Passengers who have to travel should leave extra time, because the trains will be very crowded.
Seat reservations will not be guaranteed, so we advise you to arrive early at the station.
Buses will be provided between Bath and Bristol, and they'll leave from outside the main entrance.
Staff in yellow jackets will be standing near the ticket machines to help you.
The strike is expected to end on Saturday morning, and normal service will start again that afternoon.
We apologise for any trouble and thank you for your patience.

title: Choosing a Gym Plan

lines.text: Fit Zone, Jade speaking. How can I help?
Hi, I'm thinking about joining your gym. Could you tell me about the membership options?
Of course. We have two main options. The basic one is thirty pounds a month, and the premium one is forty-five.
What's the difference between them?
With premium, you can go to the swimming pool and the sauna. The basic membership only includes the gym and the classes.
I don't swim very well, so the basic one sounds better. Are the classes busy?
The evening classes are more crowded than the morning ones, so I'd recommend going before work.
That's hard for me. I start at eight. Maybe I'll try the lunchtime yoga class.
Good choice. It's the quietest class of the day. Have you ever done yoga?
No, never. I've hurt my back twice this year, so my doctor suggested it.
Then it's perfect for you. If you sign up this week, you'll get the first month free.
That's a great offer. I'll come in tomorrow after work.

lines.text: Welcome to our class debate. Today's question is: should schools stop giving homework? Zoe, you speak first.
Thank you. I think homework should be reduced, because students need time to rest. Last week I had four tasks in one evening.
I see your point, Zoe, but I disagree. Homework helps us practise what we learn. Without it, I wouldn't remember anything.
That's true for some subjects. However, a short task is enough. Two hours every night is too much.
Maybe, although some students need more practice than others. If there were no homework, those students would fall behind.
Interesting. Can either of you suggest a compromise?
Yes. Teachers could give homework only three days a week, and nothing at the weekend.
I'd agree to that, as long as the tasks are useful and not just copying from the book.
So you both want homework, but less of it, and more meaningful. Is that right?
Exactly. Quality is better than quantity.
I couldn't agree more.

title: Three New Bins

lines.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I'd like to talk to you about recycling at our school.
Every day, our canteen throws away a lot of plastic bottles. Last term, about two hundred bottles were thrown away every week.
Many of them could be recycled, but they're put in the wrong bin.
From next Monday, three new bins will be placed in the playground: a blue one for paper, a yellow one for plastic and a green one for glass.
If you put something in the wrong bin, the whole bin can't be recycled, so please read the labels.
Class eight B has been chosen to check the bins every Friday, and they will be given a small prize.
Also, if every student brings a reusable bottle, we'll use far fewer plastic ones.
The school shop is going to sell cheap metal bottles with our school logo.
By the end of the year, we hope to reduce our rubbish by half.
Thank you for listening, and remember, small changes make a big difference.

title: Viewing a Room in a Shared Flat

Three of us at the moment, and we're looking for a fourth. Everyone has their own bedroom, but we share the kitchen and bathroom.
Sounds fair. What are the other flatmates like?
Quite easygoing. Sam works nights at a bakery, so he's usually asleep in the morning. Lena is studying for her final exams, so she needs quiet in the evenings.
That's no problem. I'm a nurse and I often work long shifts, so I'm quiet too.
Good. Do you smoke?
No, I don't, and I'd rather not live with smokers.

Not at all. I love cooking, actually. Is there a washing machine?
Yes, and a small garden, where we sometimes have barbecues in summer.

title: Weekend Weather for Campers
focus: Future forms: will, going to, might

lines.text: It's seven o'clock on Radio Coast. If you're planning a weekend in the countryside, here's Fraser with the forecast.
Thanks, Isla. Well, Friday will start sunny, but clouds are going to arrive from the west in the afternoon.
So not a great day for a picnic?
You'll probably be fine until about four. After that, there might be a few showers.
And Saturday?
That's the day to be careful. A strong wind will blow across the hills, and the rain will be heavy at times.
Would you recommend camping?
Not on the hills. If you're going to camp, choose a place near the trees, where it's more protected.
What about the temperature?
It'll be cold at night, around five degrees, so take warm sleeping bags.
And Sunday?
Much better. The sun will come out in the morning, and it should be warm and dry all day.
Fantastic. Thanks, Fraser. Stay safe, everyone.
